claim: Small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcemic type (SCCOHT) is a rare and aggressive form of ovarian cancer.
source: Small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcemic type (SCCOHT) is a rare and aggressive form of ovarian cancer.
evidence: This is a well-established characterization of SCCOHT cited in the introduction with references to published literature (Young et al., 1994; Estel et al., 2011).

claim: SCCOHT affects young women with a mean age of 24 years old.
source: Small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcemic type (SCCOHT) is a rare and aggressive form of ovarian cancer affecting young women (mean age 24 years old) (Young et al., 1994; Estel et al., 2011).
evidence: This demographic information is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: SCCOHT tumors are poorly differentiated with no known cell of origin.
source: SCCOHT tumors are poorly differentiated with no known cell of origin (Young et al., 1994).
evidence: This characterization is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Over 94% of SCCOHT tumors have mutations and concomitant protein loss of SMARCA4 (BRG1).
source: However, over 94% of SCCOHT tumors have mutations and concomitant protein loss of SMARCA4 (BRG1), one of the two mutually exclusive ATPases of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex (Karnezis et al., 2016; Clarke et al., 2016; Ramos et al., 2014a; Ramos et al., 2014b; Kupryjańczyk et al., 2013; Witkowski et al., 2014; Jelinic et al., 2014).
evidence: This frequency is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: SMARCA4 (BRG1) is one of the two mutually exclusive ATPases of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex.
source: However, over 94% of SCCOHT tumors have mutations and concomitant protein loss of SMARCA4 (BRG1), one of the two mutually exclusive ATPases of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex (Karnezis et al., 2016; Clarke et al., 2016; Ramos et al., 2014a; Ramos et al., 2014b; Kupryjańczyk et al., 2013; Witkowski et al., 2014; Jelinic et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the SWI/SNF complex supported by citations.

claim: Expression of SMARCA2 (BRM), the other ATPase, is epigenetically silenced in SCCOHT.
source: Expression of SMARCA2 (BRM), the other ATPase, is epigenetically silenced in SCCOHT, making the dual loss of both ATPases sensitive and specific for the diagnosis of SCCOHT (Karnezis et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The dual loss of both ATPases (BRG1 and BRM) is sensitive and specific for the diagnosis of SCCOHT.
source: Expression of SMARCA2 (BRM), the other ATPase, is epigenetically silenced in SCCOHT, making the dual loss of both ATPases sensitive and specific for the diagnosis of SCCOHT (Karnezis et al., 2016).
evidence: This diagnostic criterion is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: SCCOHT tumors have a simple genetic background and rarely have secondary mutations in other cancer driving genes.
source: Unlike most other adult cancers with BRG1 mutations, such as non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), SCCOHT tumors have a simple genetic background and rarely have secondary mutations in other cancer driving genes (Karnezis et al., 2016; Clarke et al., 2016; Ramos et al., 2014a; Ramos et al., 2014b; Kupryjańczyk et al., 2013; Witkowski et al., 2014; Jelinic et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2017).
evidence: This characterization is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: SCCOHT provides a unique model to understand the role that individual loss of BRG1 and the SWI/SNF complex plays in tumor development.
source: Therefore, SCCOHT provides a unique model to understand the role that individual loss of BRG1 and the SWI/SNF complex plays in tumor development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the simple genetic background of SCCOHT tumors.

claim: The SWI/SNF complex is involved in a variety of cellular processes, such as differentiation and cell cycle control.
source: The SWI/SNF complex is involved in a variety of cellular processes, such as differentiation and cell cycle control and also interacts with transcription factors (Kadam, 2000; Minderjahn et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2002), such as CMYC (Cheng et al., 1999; Weissmiller et al., 2019) and AP-1 (Vierbuchen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the SWI/SNF complex supported by citations.

claim: The SWI/SNF complex interacts with transcription factors such as CMYC and AP-1.
source: The SWI/SNF complex is involved in a variety of cellular processes, such as differentiation and cell cycle control and also interacts with transcription factors (Kadam, 2000; Minderjahn et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2002), such as CMYC (Cheng et al., 1999; Weissmiller et al., 2019) and AP-1 (Vierbuchen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: AP-1 (activator protein-1) is a dimeric transcription factor involved in many cellular processes that does not display cell type specificity.
source: AP-1 (activator protein-1) is a dimeric transcription factor involved in many cellular processes that does not display cell type specificity (Sheffield et al., 2013; Eferl and Wagner, 2003; Garces de los Fayos Alonso et al., 2018).
evidence: This characterization of AP-1 is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: AP-1 exists as either a homodimer or heterodimer transcription factor made up of a variety family members: FOS, JUN, ATF, and MAF.
source: AP-1 exists as either a homodimer or heterodimer transcription factor made up of a variety family members: FOS (c-FOS, FOSB, FRA1, FRA2), JUN (C-JUN, JUNB, JUND), ATF (ATF2, ATF3, ATF4, ATF5, ATF6, ATF6B, ATF7, BATF, BATF2, BATF3, JDP2), and MAF (c-MAF, MAFA, MAFB, MAFF, MAFG, MAFK) (Eferl and Wagner, 2003; Garces de los Fayos Alonso et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about AP-1 structure supported by citations.

claim: All AP-1 family members share a characteristic basic leucine-zipper domain (bZIP) where the DNA-binding site is located.
source: All AP-1 family members share a characteristic basic leucine-zipper domain (bZIP) where the DNA-binding site is located (Eferl and Wagner, 2003; Garces de los Fayos Alonso et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about AP-1 structure supported by citations.

claim: The first interaction described between AP-1 and SWI/SNF acted to repress transcription of c-FOS by BRG1.
source: While the first interaction described between AP-1 and SWI/SNF acted to repress transcription of c-FOS by BRG1 (Murphy et al., 1999), subsequent studies indicate positive interactions at enhancers and with more SWI/SNF subunits, such as ARID1A/B (Mathur et al., 2017; Raab et al., 2015; Kelso et al., 2017), SNF5 (Alver et al., 2017), BRM (Gao et al., 2019), and BRG1 (Vierbuchen et al., 2017; Xue et al., 2019a; Hu et al., 2011; Michel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Subsequent studies indicate positive interactions between AP-1 and SWI/SNF at enhancers and with more SWI/SNF subunits, such as ARID1A/B, SNF5, BRM, and BRG1.
source: While the first interaction described between AP-1 and SWI/SNF acted to repress transcription of c-FOS by BRG1 (Murphy et al., 1999), subsequent studies indicate positive interactions at enhancers and with more SWI/SNF subunits, such as ARID1A/B (Mathur et al., 2017; Raab et al., 2015; Kelso et al., 2017), SNF5 (Alver et al., 2017), BRM (Gao et al., 2019), and BRG1 (Vierbuchen et al., 2017; Xue et al., 2019a; Hu et al., 2011; Michel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: BRG1 reexpression in BIN67 cells induced an elongated, spindle-like morphology.
source: Following BRG1 reexpression, BIN67 showed the previously reported elongated, spindle-like morphology (Karnezis et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018) (white arrows, Figure 1b; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), whereas cells transfected with control vector displayed a similar morphology to parental cells (Figure 1b; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This morphological change is observed in the experimental data (Figure 1b) and supported by citations to previous reports.

claim: BRG1 induction resulted in growth suppression in BIN67 cells.
source: Consistent with our previous findings, BRG1 induction also resulted in growth suppression (Karnezis et al., 2016), indicated by the reduced number of cells relative to the controls (Figure 1b; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data (Figure 1b) and supported by citation to previous findings.

claim: In BIN67 RNA-seq data, 18,507 protein coding genes were identified, with 4087 genes increasing and 3444 genes decreasing following BRG1 reexpression.
source: In the BIN67 RNA-seq data, 18,507 protein coding genes were identified, with an almost equal number of genes increasing (4087 genes, 22%) and decreasing (3444 genes, 19%) (significance cut off padj <0.05) (Figure 1c; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is directly measured from RNA-seq experimental data.

claim: Genes that increased expression after BRG1 reexpression were at a greater log2 fold change and significance compared to decreasing genes.
source: In comparison to the decreasing genes, genes that increased were at a greater log2 fold change and significance (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is observed in the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: BRG1 (SMARCA4) was not the most abundantly expressed gene in the BRG1 reexpressed samples (BRG1/Control Log2FoldChange = 5.34).
source: Interestingly, BRG1 (SMARCA4) was not the most abundantly expressed gene in the BRG1 reexpressed samples (BRG1/Control Log2FoldChange = 5.34), (Figure 1c; Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is directly measured from RNA-seq experimental data.

claim: Many genes previously classified as BRG1 target genes such as CD44, EHF, IFI16, and MMP7 increased in expression after BRG1/SMARCA4 reexpression.
source: As expected, many genes previously classified as BRG1 target genes such as, CD44, EHF, IFI16, and MMP7 increased in expression after BRG1/SMARCA4 reexpression (Figure 1c; Supplementary file 1A; Strobeck et al., 2001; Reisman et al., 2002; Orvis et al., 2014; Strobeck et al., 2002).
evidence: This is observed in the RNA-seq data and supported by citations to previous studies identifying these as BRG1 target genes.

claim: Of the 5726 identified proteins in BIN67 cells, 306 proteins were significantly upregulated and 233 proteins were significantly downregulated following BRG1 reexpression.
source: Of the 5726 identified proteins, 306 proteins were significantly upregulated and 233 proteins were significantly downregulated (Figure 1d; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is directly measured from proteomics experimental data.

claim: Proteins that were upregulated after BRG1 reexpression were at a higher Log2FoldChange and significance than those downregulated.
source: Consistent with RNA-seq data, despite similar numbers of proteins increasing and decreasing after BRG1 reexpression, those that were upregulated were at a higher Log2FoldChange and significance than those downregulated.
evidence: This is observed in the proteomics data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: BRG1 (SMARCA4) was not the most upregulated protein (BRG1/Control Log2FoldChange = 3.04) following BRG1 reexpression.
source: Additionally, BRG1 (SMARCA4) was not the most upregulated protein (BRG1/Control Log2FoldChange = 3.04) (Figure 1d; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is directly measured from proteomics experimental data.

claim: CD44 protein level was significantly increased (Log2FoldChange = 2.20) following BRG1 reexpression, consistent with the increase in gene expression seen with RNA-seq.
source: CD44 protein level was significantly increased (Log2FoldChange = 2.20), consistent with the increase in gene expression seen with RNA-seq (Figure 1d; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is directly measured from proteomics and RNA-seq experimental data.

claim: There is a positive correlation (R2 = 0.407) between genes and proteins identified in both the RNA-seq and proteomics (n = 5528) in BIN67 cells.
source: Looking globally at the genes and proteins identified in both the RNA-seq and proteomics (n = 5528), we found a positive correlation (R2 = 0.407) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This correlation is calculated from the RNA-seq and proteomics experimental data.

claim: The correlation between gene and protein expression changes is stronger (R2 = 0.774) when filtered for statistically significant changes following BRG1 expression in both assays (n = 395).
source: This correlation was stronger (R2 = 0.774) when filtered for statistically significant changes following BRG1 expression in both assays (RNA-seq: padj <0.05; proteomics: FDR < 0.05; n = 395), suggesting that key gene and protein expression changes are highly correlative in BIN67 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This correlation is calculated from the RNA-seq and proteomics experimental data.

claim: Chromatin accessibility globally increased with BRG1 reexpression in BIN67 cells.
source: Overall, chromatin accessibility globally increased with BRG1 reexpression (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is observed in the ATAC-seq experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Of the 62,308 ATAC-seq peaks identified in BIN67 cells, 4023 peaks were gained and 306 peaks were lost following BRG1 reexpression.
source: Of the 62,308 ATAC-seq peaks identified, 4023 peaks were gained and 306 peaks were lost following BRG1 reexpression (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is directly measured from ATAC-seq experimental data.

claim: Control BIN67 cells most resembled immune cells such as Th2 cells and mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) based on xCell analysis.
source: Control BIN67 most resembled immune cells such as Th2 cells and mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is determined from xCell analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: BIN67 cells reexpressing BRG1 were most like epithelial cells as well as keratinocytes based on xCell analysis.
source: BIN67 cells reexpressing BRG1 were most like epithelial cells as well as keratinocytes, a specialized epithelial cell (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is determined from xCell analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Epithelial pathways were significantly enriched in the BRG1 reexpressed BIN67 cells based on GSEA for Gene Ontology (GO) terms in both RNA-seq and proteomics data.
source: In both data sets, epithelial pathways were significantly enriched in the BRG1 reexpressed cells. We identified GO terms of 'regulation of epithelial cell differentiation' in the gene expression results (Figure 2b), and GO terms of 'epithelial cell differentiation' in the proteomics results (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is determined from GSEA analysis of RNA-seq and proteomics data.

claim: A majority (60%) of the genes in the xCell epithelial list were upregulated in all three SCCOHT cell lines (BIN67, SCCOHT-1, and COV434) after BRG1 reexpression (n = 79/132 genes).
source: As expected from the xCell results for BIN67, a majority (60%) of the genes in the xCell epithelial list were upregulated in all three SCCOHT cell lines after BRG1 reexpression (n = 79/132 genes - log2FoldChange BRG1/Control > 0) (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is determined from RNA-seq data analysis across multiple SCCOHT cell lines.

claim: BIN67, SCCOHT-1, and COV434 cells reexpressing BRG1 upregulated the vast majority of the keratin genes.
source: Despite a few cell line differences, such as E-cadherin expression, we found that BIN67, SCCOHT-1, and COV434 cells reexpressing BRG1 upregulated the vast majority of the keratin genes (Figure 2e, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is observed in the RNA-seq data across multiple SCCOHT cell lines.

claim: The epithelial signature score was significantly increased after BRG1 reexpression in all three SCCOHT cell lines (BIN67, SCCOHT-1, and COV434).
source: Consistent with our previous findings, the epithelial signature score was significantly increased after BRG1 reexpression in all three SCCOHT cell lines (Welch Two Sample t-test p-values: BIN67 = 2.988e-06, COV434 = 0.0075, and SCCOHT-1 = 0.0014) (Figure 2g).
evidence: This is determined from singscore analysis of RNA-seq data with statistical testing.

claim: Of the 171 unique genes in the epithelial signature, 49 were found to have measurable gene expression and protein changes in BIN67 cells, and these were strongly correlated (R2 = 0.764).
source: Of the 171 unique genes in the epithelial signature, 49 were found to have measurable gene expression and protein changes (Figure 2h). These genes and proteins were found to be strongly correlated (R2 = 0.764) with the keratins being among the most highly upregulated in both gene and protein levels (Figure 2h).
evidence: This correlation is calculated from the RNA-seq and proteomics experimental data.

claim: The expression of both a partial (T910M) or complete (K785R) loss of catalytic activity for BRG1 in BIN67 did not induce the epithelial signature.
source: We found that the expression of both a partial (T910M) or complete (K785R) loss of catalytic activity for BRG1 in BIN67 did not induce the epithelial signature (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is determined from analysis of previously published RNA-seq data with BRG1 ATPase mutants.

claim: The induction of the epithelial gene signature by BRG1 expression in SCCOHT cells is dependent upon its catalytic activity.
source: This suggests that the induction of the epithelial gene signature by BRG1 expression in SCCOHT cells is dependent upon its catalytic activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that BRG1 ATPase mutants do not induce the epithelial signature.

claim: A427 cells significantly increased enrichment for the epithelial signature following BRG1 expression (Welch Two Sample t-test p-value=0.00067).
source: Following BRG1 expression, A427 cells significantly increased enrichment for the epithelial signature (Welch Two Sample t-test p-value=0.00067) (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is determined from singscore analysis of RNA-seq data from A427 NSCLC cells with statistical testing.

claim: In H358 cells, when BRG1 expression is lost, the score for the epithelial signature significantly decreased compared to the parent cell line (Welch Two Sample t-test p-value = 0.04437).
source: However, when BRG1 expression is lost, the score for the epithelial signature significantly decreased compared to the parent cell line (Welch Two Sample t-test p-value = 0.04437; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is determined from singscore analysis of RNA-seq data from H358 NSCLC cells with statistical testing.

claim: In H358 cells, the loss of BRM expression did not decrease the epithelial signature, rather it slightly increased it compared to the parent cell line (Welch Two Sample t-test p-value=0.02038).
source: In contrast, the loss of BRM expression did not decrease the epithelial signature, rather it slightly increased it compared to the parent cell line (Welch Two Sample t-test p-value=0.02038; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is determined from singscore analysis of RNA-seq data from H358 NSCLC cells with statistical testing.

claim: The BRG1-dependent induction of the epithelial signature appears broadly applicable to other BRG1 mutant tumors like NSCLC.
source: Together, these data indicate that the BRG1-dependent induction of the epithelial signature appears broadly applicable to other BRG1 mutant tumors like NSCLC.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that BRG1 expression induces the epithelial signature in both SCCOHT and NSCLC cell lines.

claim: There is a positive correlation (R2 = 0.41) between percentage of gained ATAC-seq peaks that overlapped with TCGA tumor types and xCell Epithelial score that was statistically significant (Pearson's correlation p-value=0.00095).
source: We found a positive correlation (R2 = 0.41) between percentage of gained ATAC-seq peaks that overlapped with xCell Epithelial score that was statistically significant (Pearson's correlation p-value=0.00095) (Figure 3c).
evidence: This correlation is calculated from comparison of ATAC-seq data with TCGA data.

claim: The altered chromatin landscape following BRG1 reexpression in BIN67 cells is similar to those of epithelial originating tumors.
source: These results indicate that the altered chromatin landscape following BRG1 reexpression in BIN67 cells is similar to those of epithelial originating tumors, consistent with our results of epithelial-like gene and protein expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the positive correlation between gained ATAC-seq peaks and xCell Epithelial scores in TCGA tumors.

claim: SCCOHT primary tumors lacked expression of Claudin-4 (average H-Score = 0).
source: SCCOHT primary tumors lacked expression of Claudin-4 (average H-Score = 0), whereas High-Grade Serous Ovarian Cancer (HGSC) tumors had a dynamic range of expression with some expressing very strongly (Figure 3e,f).
evidence: This is directly measured from immunohistochemistry staining of primary tumor tissue microarrays.

claim: SCCOHT primary tumors scored the lowest overall for CD44 expression (average CD44/DAPI: SCCOHT = 9.43%) compared to other gynecological tumors.
source: Consistent with Claudin-4 staining, SCCOHT primary tumors scored the lowest overall for CD44 expression (average CD44/DAPI: SCCOHT = 9.43%, CCOC = 34.7%, HGSC = 25.7%, LGSC = 35%, and MOC = 23.0%) (Figure 3g).
evidence: This is directly measured from immunofluorescence staining of primary tumor tissue microarrays.

claim: SCCOHT primary tumors lack the expression of select epithelial markers, consistent with findings in SCCOHT cell lines in the absence of BRG1 expression.
source: Therefore, SCCOHT primary tumors lack the expression of select epithelial markers, consistent with our findings in SCCOHT cell lines in the absence of BRG1 expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence data on primary tumors and cell line data.

claim: Chromatin accessibility was gained mostly at introns and intergenic regions after BRG1 reexpression in BIN67 cells.
source: After BRG1 reexpression, chromatin accessibility was gained mostly at introns and intergenic regions (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is determined from genomic annotation analysis of ATAC-seq data.

claim: A search for a common motif present in sites with increased chromatin accessibility showed a strong enrichment for various AP-1 family members.
source: A search for a common motif present in sites with increased chromatin accessibility showed a strong enrichment for various AP-1 family members (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is determined from transcription factor motif analysis of ATAC-seq data.

claim: The gained accessible regions in BIN67 additionally gained H3K27ac and H3K4me1 enhancer marks, defining them as enhancer regions.
source: We found that the gained accessible regions in BIN67 additionally gained H3K27ac and H3K4me1 enhancer marks, defining them as enhancer regions (Figure 4C; Pan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is determined from analysis of previously published ChIP-seq data for enhancer marks.

claim: BRG1 was recruited to sites of increased chromatin accessibility in BIN67 cells.
source: Using CUT and RUN (Skene and Henikoff, 2017), we found that BRG1 was recruited to sites of increased chromatin accessibility (Figure 4C, Supplementary file 5, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is directly measured from CUT and RUN experimental data.

claim: c-Jun was recruited to sites with increased chromatin accessibility in BIN67 cells.
source: CUT-and-RUN data for c-Jun showed strong enrichment at these sites (Figure 4C, D).
evidence: This is directly measured from CUT and RUN experimental data.

claim: There was very little c-Jun binding in BIN67 prior to BRG1 reexpression in general.
source: Notably, these regions were generally not previously bound by c-Jun in BIN67 cells. However, we noted very little c-Jun binding in BIN67 prior to BRG1 reexpression in general (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is observed in the CUT and RUN experimental data.

claim: In SCCOHT-1 cells, there was a significant amount of c-Jun relocalization following BRG1 reexpression.
source: In contrast, while c-Jun bound well prior to BRG1 reexpression in HT1 cells, there was a significant amount of c-Jun relocalization following BRG1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a)
evidence: This is observed in the CUT and RUN experimental data.

claim: Genes that newly recruited both c-Jun and BRG1 increased expression, while those that lost c-Jun and did not gain BRG1 expression decreased expression in SCCOHT-1 cells.
source: Genes that newly recruited both c-Jun and BRG1 increased expression, while those that lost c-Jun and did not gain BRG1 expression decreased expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is determined from integrated analysis of CUT and RUN and RNA-seq data.

claim: c-Jun expression was uniformly high in SCCOHT-1 cells, whereas in BIN67 c-Jun was strongly induced by BRG1 reexpression.
source: Notably c-Jun expression was uniformly high in SCCOHT-1 cells, whereas in BIN67 c-Jun was strongly induced by BRG1 reexpression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is observed in the RNA-seq data comparing BIN67 and SCCOHT-1 cells.

claim: Motifs for AP-1 family members segregated from other transcription factor motifs based on significance (p-value) and ratio of sites containing a motif over background in BRG1-bound regions in both BIN67 and SCCOHT-1 cells.
source: In both cases, motifs for AP-1 family members segregated from other transcription factor motifs based on significance (p-value) and ratio of sites containing a motif over background (Figure 4F), consistent with the ATAC-seq data (Figure 4E; Supplementary file 2B, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is determined from transcription factor motif analysis of CUT and RUN data.

claim: At promoter regions containing FRA1 motifs, ATAC-seq signal mostly remained open with a small number of sites opening after BRG1 reexpression.
source: At promoter regions, ATAC-seq signal mostly remained open with a small number of sites opening after BRG1 reexpression (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is observed in the ATAC-seq data at FRA1 motif sites.

claim: At distal regions containing a FRA1 site, nearly all locations gained chromatin accessibility and enhancer marks (H3K27ac and H3K4me1) after BRG1 reexpression.
source: However, at distal regions containing a FRA1 site, nearly all locations gained chromatin accessibility and enhancer marks (H3K27ac and H3K4me1) after BRG1 reexpression (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is observed in the ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq data at FRA1 motif sites.

claim: BRG1 was recruited to FRA1 locations at both promoter and distal regions.
source: For both promoter and distal regions, BRG1 was recruited to FRA1 locations (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is observed in the CUT and RUN data at FRA1 motif sites.

claim: AP-1 family member c-Jun was strongly recruited to its motifs present in both promoter proximal and distal open chromatin.
source: AP-1 family member c-Jun was also strongly recruited to its motifs present in both promoter proximal and distal open chromatin (Figure 4g).
evidence: This is observed in the CUT and RUN data at AP-1 motif sites.

claim: AP-1 is a common motif associated with BRG1 both at promoter and distal locations, implicating AP-1 transcriptional control as an important mediator of SCCOHT development.
source: Consistent with previous reports of AP-1 and SWI/SNF interactions (Vierbuchen et al., 2017), these results suggested that AP-1 is a common motif associated with BRG1 both at promoter and distal locations, implicating AP-1 transcriptional control as an important mediator of SCCOHT development.
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment of AP-1 motifs at BRG1-bound regions and supported by citation to previous reports.

claim: A bimodal distribution of expression changes was observed for the epithelial genes in both BIN67 and SCCOHT-1 cells.
source: We found a bimodal distribution of expression changes (Figure 5A). This was observed in both BIN67and SCCOHT-1 cells with a strong concordance in the expression levels of the epithelial signature in both cell lines (Pearson's r = 0.66, p-value=3.95e−22, Figure 5B).
evidence: This is observed in the RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: There is a strong concordance in the expression levels of the epithelial signature in both BIN67 and SCCOHT-1 cell lines (Pearson's r = 0.66, p-value=3.95e−22).
source: This was observed in both BIN67and SCCOHT-1 cells with a strong concordance in the expression levels of the epithelial signature in both cell lines (Pearson's r = 0.66, p-value=3.95e−22, Figure 5B).
evidence: This correlation is calculated from RNA-seq data comparing BIN67 and SCCOHT-1 cells.

claim: The epithelial low group was strongly enriched in ZEB1/2 transcription factor motifs.
source: The epithelial low group was strongly enriched in ZEB1/2 transcription factor motifs, not surprising given their well-characterized role in regulating EMT/epithelial cells (Lamouille et al., 2014; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is determined from transcription factor motif analysis at promoters of epithelial low genes and supported by citation to literature on ZEB1/2 function.

claim: The epithelial high group showed a strong enrichment in AP-1 family members at promoter regions.
source: However, the epithelial high group showed a strong enrichment in AP-1 family members (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is determined from transcription factor motif analysis at promoters of epithelial high genes.

claim: Chromatin accessibility increased more for the high epithelial group than for the low epithelial group and non-epithelial groups at BRG1 CUT and RUN peaks.
source: ATAC-seq signal (log2FoldChange; BRG1/Control) was determined at BRG1 CUT and RUN peaks in BIN67 that are annotated to epithelial low, epithelial high, or non-epithelial genes (Figure 5d). Chromatin accessibility increased more for the high epithelial group than for the low epithelial group and non-epithelial groups (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is determined from integrated analysis of ATAC-seq and CUT and RUN data.

claim: Strong recruitment of both BRG1 and c-Jun can be seen near the promoters and in upstream regions of epithelial high genes such as S100A2 and SFN.
source: At individual loci, strong recruitment of both BRG1 and c-Jun can be seen near the promoters and in upstream regions of genes (Figure 5d, S100A2 and SFN).
evidence: This is observed in the CUT and RUN data shown in genome browser tracks.

claim: The increased expression of the epithelial high genes in BIN67 depends upon BRG1 recruitment and chromatin remodeling combined with the activity of AP-1.
source: These results collectively support the concept that the increased expression of the epithelial high genes in BIN67 depends upon BRG1 recruitment and chromatin remodeling combined with the activity of AP-1.
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment of AP-1 motifs at epithelial high gene promoters, increased chromatin accessibility, and recruitment of both BRG1 and c-Jun.

claim: The gene expression of many members corresponding to each of the four main AP-1 families (FOS, JUN, ATF, MAF) were upregulated after BRG1 reexpression in BIN67 and SCCOHT-1 cells.
source: We found that the gene expression of many members corresponding to each of the four main families (FOS, JUN, ATF, MAF) were upregulated after BRG1 reexpression in BIN67 and SCCOHT-1 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is observed in the RNA-seq data.

claim: BIN67 pIND20-FLAG-A-FOS (-DOX condition; absence of A-FOS) cells +/- BRG1 recapitulated the parental BIN67 +/- BRG1 by a strong correlation (R2 = 0.724, Pearson's Correlation p-value<2.2e-16) in log2FoldChange for the 767 statistically significant genes.
source: We found that BIN67 pIND20-FLAG-A-FOS (-DOX condition; absence of A-FOS) cells +/- BRG1 recapitulated the parental BIN67 +/- BRG1 by a strong correlation (R2 = 0.724, Pearson's Correlation p-value<2.2e-16) in log2FoldChange for the 767 statistically significant genes (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This correlation is calculated from RNA-seq data comparing parental and inducible cell lines.

claim: All control transfected conditions clustered together in PCA analysis, regardless of the induction of A-FOS.
source: Unsupervised principal component analysis of the four conditions (+/- BRG1, +/- DOX(A-FOS)) in BIN67 pIND20-FLAG-A-FOS showed that that all control transfected conditions clustered together (blue), regardless of the induction of A-FOS (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is observed in the PCA analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: BRG1 transfected conditions segregated separately based on the presence or absence of DOX (A-FOS) in PCA analysis.
source: However, BRG1 transfected conditions segregated separately based on the presence or absence of DOX (A-FOS) (red), in addition to segregating from control transfected samples (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is observed in the PCA analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: The induction of A-FOS had little to no effect on control transfected BIN67 cells, with only eight genes significantly upregulated and 24 genes significantly downregulated.
source: The little to no effect that the induction in of A-FOS had on control transfected cells was confirmed with differential expression analysis of RNA-seq data where only eight genes were significantly upregulated and 24 genes were significantly downregulated (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C; Supplementary file 3B).
evidence: This is determined from differential expression analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: The induction of A-FOS had a greater effect on BRG1 reexpressed cells, with 405 genes significantly downregulated and 52 significantly upregulated.
source: However, as expected with the PCA analysis, the induction of A-FOS had a greater effect on BRG1 reexpressed cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D). We found that more genes were downregulated upon A-FOS induction than upregulated when BRG1 was reexpressed (405 significantly downregulated and 52 significantly upregulated) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D; Supplementary file 3C).
evidence: This is determined from differential expression analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Of the 405 genes that were downregulated in the presence of A-FOS (+DOX) and BRG1 reexpression, nearly all these genes were upregulated by BRG1 in BIN67 parental cell line and BIN67 pIND20-FLAG-A-FOS, -DOX conditions.
source: Of the 405 genes that were downregulated in the presence of A-FOS (+DOX) and BRG1 reexpression, nearly all these genes were upregulated by BRG1 in BIN67 parental cell line and BIN67 pIND20-FLAG-A-FOS, -DOX conditions (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is determined from integrated analysis of RNA-seq data across conditions.

claim: BRG1 is necessary for nearly all AP-1-dependent gene changes in BIN67 cells.
source: Since AFOS induction alone had little effect on BIN67 cells and the greatest changes were seen with both the reexpression of BRG1 and induction of A-FOS, we determined that BRG1 is necessary for nearly all AP-1-dependent gene changes in BIN67 cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that A-FOS induction has minimal effect without BRG1 reexpression.

claim: The induction of A-FOS with BRG1 expression mitigated the increase of many, but not all BRG1-dependent gene expression in BIN67 cells.
source: We found that the induction of A-FOS with BRG1 expression mitigated the increase of many, but not all BRG1-dependent gene expression in BIN67 cells (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is observed in the RNA-seq data comparing BRG1 expression with and without A-FOS induction.

claim: There was a decrease in most expression levels of the epithelial genes when both BRG1 and A-FOS were induced in BIN67, as compared to BRG1 induction alone.
source: We found a decrease in most expression levels of the epithelial genes when both BRG1 and A-FOS were induced in BIN67, as compared to BRG1 induction alone (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is observed in the RNA-seq data for epithelial signature genes.

claim: Most, but not all BRG1 dependent gene expression changes require AP-1 activity.
source: Thus, most, but not all BRG1 dependent gene expression changes require AP-1 activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that A-FOS induction reduces but does not eliminate BRG1-dependent gene expression changes.

claim: BRG1 reexpression in BIN67 parental cells and BIN67 pIND20-FLAG-A-FOS (-DOX conditions) induced CD44 protein expression.
source: BRG1 reexpression in BIN67 parental cells and BIN67 pIND20-FLAG-A-FOS (-DOX conditions) induced CD44 protein expression (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is directly observed in western blot data.

claim: In the presence of A-FOS and BRG1 expression, CD44 protein expression was absent.
source: In the presence of A-FOS and BRG1 expression, CD44 protein expression was absent (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is directly observed in western blot data.

claim: Following BRG1 reexpression in BIN67 parental cells and BIN67 pIND20-FLAG-A-FOS (-DOX conditions; A-FOS absent), Claudin-4 expression increased at protein levels.
source: Following BRG1 reexpression in BIN67 parental cells and BIN67 pIND20-FLAG-A-FOS (-DOX conditions; A-FOS absent), Claudin-4 expression increased protein (Figure 6e) levels.
evidence: This is directly observed in western blot data.

claim: In the presence of A-FOS and BRG1 expression, Claudin-4 protein expression was lost.
source: However, in the presence of A-FOS and BRG1 expression, Claudin-4 protein expression was lost (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is directly observed in western blot data.

claim: Global gene expression of epithelial targets induced by BRG1 depended upon the activity of AP-1.
source: In summary, we observed that global gene expression of epithelial targets induced by BRG1 depended upon the activity of AP-1.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq data showing reduced epithelial gene expression when A-FOS is induced with BRG1.

claim: Both active AP-1 and BRG1 reexpression in BIN67 are necessary for the induction of epithelial targets, suggesting that neither alone is sufficient to induce their expression.
source: Thus, both active AP-1 and BRG1 reexpression in BIN67 are necessary for the induction of epithelial targets, suggesting that neither alone is sufficient to induce their expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that epithelial protein expression requires both BRG1 and active AP-1.

claim: After BRG1 reexpression, chromatin accessibility is gained at distal enhancer regions enriched with AP-1 motifs accompanied by recruitment of BRG1.
source: These results support a model where after BRG1 reexpression, chromatin accessibility is gained at distal enhancer regions enriched with AP-1 motifs accompanied by recruitment of BRG1 (Figure 7).
evidence: This model is inferred from the integrated multi-omic data showing AP-1 motif enrichment, chromatin accessibility changes, and BRG1 recruitment.

claim: BRG1 is recruited to the promoters of epithelial genes that contain AP-1 motifs.
source: Additionally, BRG1 is recruited to the promoters of epithelial genes that contain AP-1 motifs (Figure 7).
evidence: This is observed in the CUT and RUN data and motif analysis.

claim: BRG1 and AP-1 together have an important biological impact on inducing an epithelial-like signature in SCCOHT cells.
source: Our results demonstrate that BRG1 and AP-1 together have an important biological impact on inducing an epithelial-like signature in SCCOHT cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results showing that both BRG1 and AP-1 activity are necessary for epithelial gene and protein expression.

claim: Associations between AP-1 and various SWI/SNF complex members at enhancer regions have been previously described, such as ARID1A/B in colorectal cancer and ovarian clear cell carcinoma and SNF5 in malignant rhabdoid tumors.
source: Associations between AP-1 and various SWI/SNF complex members at enhancer regions have been previously described, such as ARID1A/B (Mathur et al., 2017; Raab et al., 2015; Kelso et al., 2017) in colorectal cancer and ovarian clear cell carcinoma and SNF5 (Alver et al., 2017) in malignant rhabdoid tumors.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: BRG1 and AP-1 associations have been shown globally at enhancer sites in mouse embryonic fibroblasts, mouse mammary epithelial cells, and described specifically for CCND1 in NSCLC and in AML.
source: Specifically, BRG1 and AP-1 associations have been shown globally at enhancer sites in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (Vierbuchen et al., 2017), mouse mammary epithelial cells (Hu et al., 2011), and described specifically for CCND1 in NSCLC (Xue et al., 2019a) and in AML (Michel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The current study provides the first insight into the biological significance of the BRG1 and AP-1 mechanism showing that BRG1 reexpression in SCCOHT cell lines drives an epithelial-like gene and protein signature.
source: Our results are consistent with these reports and provide the first insight into the biological significance of this mechanism showing that BRG1 reexpression in SCCOHT cell lines drives an epithelial-like gene and protein signature.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the current study's findings.

claim: AP-1 has been suggested as a pioneer transcription factor for its ability to bind to closed chromatin and promote chromatin accessibility for the glucocorticoid receptor in mouse mammary epithelial cells.
source: Much like the Vierbuchen et al. model, AP-1 has been suggested by others as a pioneer transcription factor for its ability to bind to closed chromatin and promote chromatin accessibility for the glucocorticoid receptor in mouse mammary epithelial cells (Biddie et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: In SCCOHT-1 cells, at c-Jun sites present prior to BRG1 expression, recruitment of BRG1 did not enhance gene expression.
source: Additionally, we found in SCCOHT-1 cells that at c-Jun sites present prior to BRG1 expression, recruitment of BRG1 did not enhance gene expression.
evidence: This is observed in the integrated analysis of CUT and RUN and RNA-seq data.

claim: Only sites that newly recruited c-Jun and BRG1 upregulated gene expression in SCCOHT-1 cells.
source: Only sites that newly recruited c-Jun and BRG1 upregulated gene expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in the integrated analysis of CUT and RUN and RNA-seq data.

claim: BRG1 localized to promoters and presumptive enhancer regions following BRG1 reexpression, consistent with previous reports in other cell types.
source: In our study, BRG1 localized to promoters and presumptive enhancer regions following BRG1 reexpression. This result is consistent with previous reports in other cell types of BRG1 recruitment to promoter regions (Tolstorukov et al., 2013) and to distal enhancer regions (Alver et al., 2017; Hu et al., 2011; Morris et al., 2014; Agaimy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is observed in the CUT and RUN data and supported by citations to previous reports.

claim: AP-1 co-localization with other transcription factors in enhancer regions depends on cell lineage.
source: As suggested recently, AP-1 co-localization with other transcription factors in enhancer regions depends on cell lineage (Vierbuchen et al., 2017), such as AP-1 and TEAD in MEFs (Vierbuchen et al., 2017) and breast cancer cells (Zanconato et al., 2015) and AP-1 and ETS family members in oesophageal adenocarcinoma (Britton et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In the control BIN67 cells, there was a strong similarity to MSC by xCell cell type enrichment analysis.
source: In the control BIN67 cells, we found a strong similarity to MSC by xCell cell type enrichment analysis.
evidence: This is determined from xCell analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: The loss of BRG1 and the SWI/SNF complex may result in an epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) or may prevent cells during early development from developing into epithelial tissue.
source: This finding suggests that the loss of BRG1 and the SWI/SNF complex may result in an epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) or may prevent cells during early development from developing into epithelial tissue.
evidence: This is speculated based on the MSC-like signature in control BIN67 cells.

claim: In NSCLC, EMT is associated with poorer prognosis and disease progression.
source: As seen in NSCLC, another adult cancer where BRG1 loss is a progressive event, EMT is associated with poorer prognosis and disease progression (Tsoukalas et al., 2017; Mahmood et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: BRG1 loss in cancer may have a more universal role in driving EMT and leading to tumor development or progression.
source: Given the aggressiveness and poor prognosis for SCCOHT tumors, our results suggest a more universal role of BRG1 loss in cancer in driving EMT and leading to tumor development or progression.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings in SCCOHT and comparison to NSCLC.

claim: SCCOHT tumors may arise from an epithelial-like cell.
source: In addition to the novel biological mechanism between AP-1 and BRG1 driving epithelial-like differentiation, our work indicates that SCCOHT tumors may arise from an epithelial-like cell.
evidence: This is speculated based on the epithelial signature induced by BRG1 reexpression.

claim: Four primary SCCOHT tumors stained for CLDN4 were negative by IHC in the initial study by Schaefer et al., 2017.
source: In the initial study by Schaefer et al., 2017, four primary SCCOHT tumors stained for CLDN4 were negative by IHC (Schaefer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: A second study by Tessier-Cloutier et al., 2018, found frequent lack of CLDN4 expression in dedifferentiated and undifferentiated endometrial carcinomas despite having a known epithelial origin.
source: However, a second study by Tessier-Cloutier et al., 2018, looking at dedifferentiated and undifferentiated endometrial carcinomas, found frequent lack of CLDN4 expression despite having a known epithelial origin, suggesting that CLDN4 may not be used to infer epithelial origin in undifferentiated endometrial tumors (Tessier-Cloutier et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The loss of CLDN4 in primary SCCOHT tumors does not rule out an epithelial origin.
source: Thus, the loss of CLDN4 in primary SCCOHT tumors does not rule out an epithelial origin.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that undifferentiated tumors of known epithelial origin can lack CLDN4 expression.

claim: BIN67 parental cell line does not express CLDN4 at both transcript and protein levels, much like the primary SCCOHT tumors.
source: Our data is consistent with Tessier-Cloutier et al. and Schaefer et al. in that BIN67 parental cell line does not express CLDN4 at both transcript and protein levels, much like the primary SCCOHT tumors.
evidence: This is observed in the RNA-seq and western blot data.

claim: When BRG1 is reexpressed in BIN67 cells, the cells become more differentiated and express CLDN4, suggesting an epithelial cell origin.
source: When BRG1 is reexpressed in BIN67 cells, the cells become more differentiated and express CLDN4, suggesting an epithelial cell origin.
evidence: This is observed in the RNA-seq and western blot data and used to infer epithelial origin.

claim: Some pathological analyses of primary SCCOHT samples suggest that it arises from an immature teratoma.
source: Of interest, some pathological analyses of primary SCCOHT samples suggest that it arises from an immature teratoma (Kupryjańczyk et al., 2013; McCluggage et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: An epithelial cell in one of the tissues compromising immature teratoma gives rise to a SCCOHT tumor, although the tissue type within the immature teratoma cannot be defined.
source: With the addition of our data, it would suggest that an epithelial cell in one of the tissues compromising immature teratoma gives rise to a SCCOHT tumor, although we cannot define the tissue type within the immature teratoma.
evidence: This is speculated based on the epithelial signature findings and previous reports of teratoma origin.
